title: Chapter 10 — A Bosom Friend
paragraphs: Returning to the Spouter-Inn from the Chapel, I found Queequeg there alone. He'd left the service before the benediction. He was sitting on a bench by the fire with his feet on the stove hearth, holding his little idol close to his face, peering hard into it and gently whittling its nose with a jackknife, meanwhile humming to himself in his heathen way.

When I interrupted him, he put the idol away. Soon he went to the table, picked up a large book, placed it on his lap, and began counting the pages with careful regularity. Every fifty pages or so, he'd stop, look vaguely around, and let out a long, gurgling whistle of astonishment. Then he'd start again at the next fifty, seeming to begin at one each time, as if he couldn't count past fifty — and it was only the sheer number of fifties that amazed him.

I watched him with great interest. Savage though he was, and hideously scarred about the face — at least to my taste — there was something in his expression that wasn't at all disagreeable. You can't hide the soul. Through all his unearthly tattoos, I thought I could see traces of a simple, honest heart. And in his large, deep eyes — fiery black and bold — there were signs of a spirit that would dare a thousand devils. Beyond all this, there was a certain dignity about the man that even his roughness couldn't destroy. He looked like someone who had never groveled and never owed a debt. Whether it was because his shaved head made his forehead stand out in clearer, broader relief, I won't say — but his head was phrenologically excellent. Ridiculous as it may sound, it reminded me of General Washington's head, as you see it in popular busts: the same long, evenly sloping forehead retreating from projecting brows that jutted out like two wooded promontories. Queequeg was George Washington, cannibalistically developed.

While I studied him closely — half-pretending to watch the storm through the window — he never noticed me at all. He appeared completely absorbed in counting the pages of that marvelous book. Considering how sociably we'd slept together the night before, and especially the affectionate arm I'd found thrown over me that morning, his indifference seemed very strange. But savages are strange beings. Sometimes you don't know how to take them. At first they're overawing; their calm self-possession seems like Socratic wisdom. I'd also noticed that Queequeg never mingled with the other sailors at the inn. He made no effort to widen his circle of acquaintances. All this struck me as remarkable, yet on second thought, there was something almost sublime about it. Here was a man twenty thousand miles from home — by way of Cape Horn, the only route available to him — thrown among people as alien to him as if he'd landed on Jupiter. Yet he seemed completely at ease, perfectly serene, content with his own company, always equal to himself. Surely this was a touch of fine philosophy, even though he'd probably never heard such a thing existed. But perhaps to be true philosophers, we mortals shouldn't be conscious of living or striving as such. The moment I hear someone calls himself a philosopher, I conclude that, like the dyspeptic old woman, he must have broken his digester.

As I sat in that now-lonely room — the fire burning low, in that gentle stage when, having warmed the air, it just glows to be looked at; the evening shadows and phantoms gathering at the windows, peering in at us, a silent, solitary pair; the storm booming outside in solemn swells — I began to feel strange sensations. Something was melting in me. My splintered heart and furious fist were no longer turned against the wolfish world. This soothing savage had redeemed it. There he sat, his very indifference revealing a nature free of civilized hypocrisies and smooth deceits. Wild he was — a sight of sights to see. Yet I began to feel myself mysteriously drawn to him. And the very things that would have repelled most people were the magnets that attracted me. I'll try a pagan friend, I thought, since Christian kindness has proved to be hollow courtesy. I moved my bench closer and made friendly signs and hints, doing my best to talk with him. At first he barely noticed, but when I mentioned his hospitality the night before, he managed to ask whether we'd be bedfellows again. I said yes, and he seemed pleased — perhaps a little flattered.

We turned over the book together, and I tried to explain the purpose of printing and the meaning of the few pictures in it. This caught his interest, and from there we moved on to chattering as best we could about the various sights to see in this famous town. Soon I suggested we smoke together. He produced his pouch and tomahawk-pipe and quietly offered me a puff. And then we sat, exchanging puffs from that wild pipe of his, passing it regularly back and forth.

If there still lingered any ice of indifference between us, that friendly pipe thawed it away. He seemed to feel a warm regard for me from the start, and when our smoke was over, he pressed his forehead against mine, clasped me around the waist, and said that from now on we were married — meaning, in his country's way, that we were bosom friends. He would gladly die for me, if need be. In a country where they don't regulate these things by law, I suppose they use this simple, savage way. In any case, he seemed to consider us joined.

After supper, we went up to our room together. He brought out his giant tobacco pouch, which also served as a pillow — with the tomahawk he smoked with tucked inside. He offered me the pillow and the tomahawk-pipe, and we sat together on the edge of the bed. He then produced about thirty dollars in silver, spread them on the table, divided them into two equal piles, pushed one toward me, and insisted I keep it. I tried to refuse, but he swept it into my trousers pocket. He then went through a sort of ceremony, emptied his pipe's ashes, held up his idol, and made a ritual of fire — offering me the idol to worship along with him.

I was a good Christian, born and bred in the bosom of the infallible Presbyterian Church. How then could I unite with this wild idolator in worshipping his piece of wood? But what is worship? thought I. Do you suppose now, Ishmael, that the magnanimous God of heaven and earth — pagans and all included — can possibly be jealous of an insignificant bit of black wood? Impossible! But what is worship? — to do the will of God — that is worship. And what is the will of God? — to do to my fellow man what I would have my fellow man to do to me — that is the will of God. Now, Queequeg is my fellow man. And what do I wish that this Queequeg would do to me? Why, unite with me in my particular Presbyterian form of worship. Consequently, I must then unite with him in his; ergo, I must turn idolator. So I kindled the shavings; helped prop up the innocent little idol; offered him burnt biscuit with Queequeg; salamed before him twice or thrice; kissed his nose; and that done, we undressed and went to bed, at peace with our own consciences and all the world. But we did not go to sleep without some little chat.

How it is I know not; but there is no place like a bed for confidential disclosures between friends. Man and wife, they say, there open the very bottom of their souls to each other; and some old couples often lie and chat over old times till nearly morning. Thus, then, in our hearts' honeymoon, lay I and Queequeg — a cozy, loving pair.
